description: Signed messages that carry what neither implementation will construct: a certificate thumbprint labelled with an algorithm that is not a hash algorithm, or with one that is and that neither of them computes (§24, normative but for the SHA-1 row), a certificate written down in an encoding that is not DER (§25, normative since 2026-11-02), and a certificate source neither implementation reads — x5bag and x5u (§26, normative where an unread header must not cost a sound message its verification, survey where a verifier that read the label would be right to answer differently), and a certificate whose signature algorithm carries a parameter RFC 4055 §5 does not allow, consistently in both of the copies a certificate holds — which no patch can reach, so this family mints its certificate and signs it (§28, normative where RFC 4055 puts the rule on the reader in its own words, survey where the two disagree). Generated by tools/X509Cases from the noble primitives and the RSA written out in it; the chain, the signing key and the issuing key come from cose-x509-corpus.json, and three families' controls are byte for byte messages both implementations produce. Each case states how many certificates it carries and whether they are DER; tools/DerArbiter answers both with a reader that is neither implementation's, which is what §25's rows had no third opinion about.

cases.description: The control, and the one of these five messages that neither implementation refuses: the x5t header names SHA-256, the hash algorithm the digest beside it was computed with. Its bytes are not this generator's word for what a sound message looks like — they are byte for byte the message both implementations produce and agree on for `cose-x509:thumbprint-names-the-certificate`, and the generator refuses to write this file unless it reproduces them. Without this row the three refusals beside it would prove nothing: a message that verifies for nobody is refused by everybody, whatever they check.

cases.reason: x5t carries a hash, and ES256 is a signature algorithm, not a hash algorithm
cases.description: The same message, with one CBOR integer changed: the x5t header labels the thumbprint ES256. The digest beside it is still the correct SHA-256 of the end-entity certificate, so an implementation that reads the digest and computes SHA-256 without looking at the label finds a match and verifies the message — which is what makes refusing it a measurable answer rather than the only possible one. ES256 names SHA-256 for the signature it makes, and RFC 9360 §2 gives x5t a hash; a thumbprint that named ES256 would claim a computation nobody performed. No error text is judged: failing to read the message counts as refusing it, and verifying it is the one wrong answer.

cases.reason: x5t carries a hash, and HMAC 256/256 is a MAC algorithm, not a hash algorithm
cases.description: The same message again, labelling the thumbprint HMAC 256/256. It stands beside the ES256 row rather than duplicating it: HMAC 256/256 also names SHA-256, for the tag it computes, so an implementation that refuses only signature algorithms passes the row before this one and fails here. The digest is again the correct SHA-256 of the end-entity certificate.

cases.reason: x5t carries a hash, and ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 is a key agreement algorithm, not a hash algorithm
cases.description: The third of the same message, labelling the thumbprint ECDH-ES + HKDF-256. It names SHA-256 for the key derivation it performs, so the three rows together separate an implementation that asks whether an algorithm has a digest — which all three do — from one that asks whether it is a hash algorithm, which is what RFC 9054 registers and what both implementations check. The first kind verifies all three messages.

cases.reason: the thumbprint is a correct SHA-1 of the certificate, and neither implementation computes SHA-1
cases.description: The fourth label after the control, and the first one here that really is a hash algorithm: SHA-1, which RFC 9054 §3.1 registers for exactly this field and recommends "Filter Only" - which the registry defines as not for purposes that require collision resistance. So the digest beside it is not the SHA-256 of the three rows above but the correct SHA-1 of the end-entity certificate, a value neither implementation can compute, which is why a third encoder has to write it. The question is therefore a different one: not whether an implementation checks that the label names a hash algorithm, but what it does with a hash algorithm it does not have. Verifying is one wrong answer; silently ignoring the thumbprint is the dangerous one, because a verifier that skips a check it cannot perform accepts the chain the thumbprint was there to pin. Measured: both refuse, and both say the same thing. Until this row existed that sentence was that SHA-1 is not a hash algorithm, which is false; since COSE.TS 87264c2 and Styx 59211b99 it is that SHA-1 is a hash algorithm they do not compute. No error text is judged in this family either way - the verdict is the row, and FINDINGS §24 keeps the record of the wording. `survey`, because the premise is a reading and a property of these two rather than a rule: RFC 9054 keeps SHA-1 registered for the situations that still need it, naming historic HSMs and filtering, where collision resistance is not needed - and an implementation that computed it and took x5t for a filter would be within the specification verifying this message. Whether a thumbprint beside a sound chain is a filter or a binding check is what the class leaves open, and it is for the specification to settle rather than for this suite.

cases.encoding: both certificates as tools/CertificateCorpus minted them
cases.description: The control of this family, on the same argument as the thumbprint control above: its bytes are byte for byte the message both implementations produce and agree on for `cose-x509:chain-to-trusted-root`, and the generator refuses to write this file unless it reproduces them. So the refusals below are refusals of a sound message with one certificate written down differently, and of nothing else — not of a construction this generator got wrong.

cases.reason: the certificate's outer length is `83 00 01 4E`, three octets where two suffice, and DER writes a length in the fewest octets that hold it
cases.encoding: the certificate at position 0 of the chain, with a leading zero in its outer length
cases.description: The end-entity certificate, written down with a length that is not DER. The tampering is outside the TBSCertificate, so the issuer's signature over it still holds and the chain still reaches the anchor: an implementation that does not check the encoding verifies this message. Bouncy Castle read it before Styx f1057ea8; COSE.TS refuses it at the length octets.

cases.reason: the certificate is wrapped in `30 80` … `00 00`, which is BER and not DER, and RFC 5280 §4.1 requires DER
cases.encoding: the certificate at position 0 of the chain, with an indefinite outer length
cases.description: The same certificate with an indefinite length, which is the one tampering here that a reader cannot start accepting by leaving a check out — it has to implement BER to get through it at all. That this row opens is therefore not argued from a mutilated reader but measured on a shipped one: Bouncy Castle read this certificate, and Styx verified this message, before f1057ea8.

cases.reason: one octet follows the certificate inside the x5chain byte string, and an x5chain entry carries one certificate and nothing else
cases.encoding: the certificate at position 0 of the chain, with one byte appended after it
cases.description: The certificate followed by a byte that is not part of it. A parser that reads the first certificate and stops — which is what `X509CertificateParser.ReadCertificate` does — never sees that byte, so this is the row that asks whether what arrived was read to its end. COSE.TS insists on it in `DerReader.expectEnd`.

cases.reason: the signatureAlgorithm's length is `81 0A` where `0A` suffices, so a length inside the certificate is not DER although the outer one is
cases.encoding: the certificate at position 0 of the chain, with a long-form length in its signatureAlgorithm
cases.description: The length that is not DER sits inside the certificate rather than in its outer header, which separates a reader that validates the record it was handed from one that validates every record in it: the first passes the leading-zero row above and fails this one. The outer length is recomputed, so the certificate is well formed apart from that single field.

cases.reason: one octet follows the certification authority's certificate, at position 1 of the chain, and every entry of an x5chain carries one certificate
cases.encoding: the certificate at position 1 of the chain, with one byte appended after it
cases.description: The same appended byte, one position further up the chain. An implementation that checks the encoding of the certificate a message is about and then parses the rest of the chain however it can passes every row above and verifies this one. Styx f1057ea8 names the position in its refusal for that reason.

cases.reason: the certificate is not DER, which is reason enough before any thumbprint is compared — and this thumbprint is the honest hash of the bytes that travelled
cases.encoding: the certificate at position 0 of the chain, with a leading zero in its outer length
cases.description: The second question §25 asked. x5t is the hash of a certificate's DER encoding [RFC 9360, Section 2], so when a parser accepts an encoding that is not DER, which bytes does it hash? Here the thumbprint is the hash of exactly what is in the message, so an implementation that reads the certificate leniently and hashes what it was given finds a match and verifies — COSE.TS hashes the record as it appeared, and would. The tampering is the leading zero rather than the indefinite length precisely so that this row has a demonstrated opening and not an argued one.

cases.reason: the certificate is not DER, and the thumbprint names its canonical encoding, which is not what travelled
cases.encoding: the certificate at position 0 of the chain, with a leading zero in its outer length
cases.thumbprintOver: the canonical DER, which is not in the message
cases.description: The same certificate, with x5t over the canonical DER of it — a byte string that is not in this message and that the sender never sent. An implementation that reads the certificate leniently and hashes its own re-encoding finds a match here and verifies: that is Styx before f1057ea8, where `GetEncoded()` returned Bouncy Castle's encoding rather than the bytes read. Together with the row before it, this pins the refusal to the certificate: a lenient reader hashes either what it got or what it re-encoded, and each of those two verifies one of these two rows, so both green means the certificate itself was refused.

cases.reason: the certificates are in an x5bag (label 32), which is a heap and not a path, and nothing in the message says which of them signed it
cases.headers: x5bag with the chain in it, and no x5chain
cases.description: The end-entity certificate and the authority above it in an x5bag, and no x5chain anywhere in the message. The bytes in the bag are the chain of the control, in the same order, so an implementation that reads label 32 the way it reads 33 walks them to the anchor and verifies this message — which is what makes a refusal an answer rather than the only possibility. Both refuse today, because neither reads the label. `survey` and not `normative` for the reason §25 gives: RFC 9360 §2 describes building a path from a bag rather than requiring it, gives no rule for which certificate in a bag signed, and requires only that the end-entity certificate be integrity protected — which the bag here is, by sitting in the protected bucket. So an implementation that read label 32 would be within the specification verifying this message, and whether an unordered heap may serve as evidence is for the specification to settle rather than for this suite. What the row records is how each side reads a label it has a name for and no reader for.

cases.headers: x5bag with a path to the anchor that is not the signer's, beside the chain
cases.description: The sound chain in x5chain, and in an x5bag beside it a path that is not the signer's: `strangerMeter` under the same authority, which leads to the same trusted root and certifies a key that did not sign this message — the certificate `cose-x509:chain-certifies-another-key` is built from. So the bag is not nonsense a verifier can dismiss on sight. An implementation that prefers it, or that merges it into the chain and starts at the first entry it finds, validates a chain beautifully, reaches the anchor, and then holds the wrong key: it refuses a message whose own chain is sound. RFC 9052 §3 says a header parameter that is neither critical nor understood is ignored, so this row is `normative` — and it stays right whoever implements what, because a bag beside a chain is extra evidence and never a substitute for it.

cases.reason: crit names label 32 and neither implementation understands x5bag, and RFC 9052 §3.1 gives a verifier that cannot process a critical header nothing to do but refuse
cases.headers: x5bag with one certificate, beside the chain, with crit [32]
cases.description: The sound chain, an x5bag holding the single stranger certificate — the one-certificate form of COSE_X509, a byte string and not an array — and `crit: [32]`, by which the sender says to refuse this message unless the verifier understands x5bag. The same message without that one entry verifies on both sides, measured rather than argued (§26), which is what makes the refusal measurable — a verifier that ignores crit, or that counts a label it can name as a label it understands, verifies here. `cose-crit:crit-unknown-label` asks this with label 32767, which nobody can ever understand; this asks it with a registered label both implementations have a name for, which is the version a verifier gets wrong by accident. `normative` since 2026-11-02: the message meets every structural requirement RFC 9052 §3.1 makes of a crit — the label and the crit itself are in the protected bucket, the array holds a value — so what is left of §3.1 here is its demand that a listed label be *processed*, and neither of these two processes label 32. For a verifier that does not, refusing is what §3.1 prescribes rather than what it prefers. One that grew a reader for x5bag would understand the label and would be right to accept: this row is to be read again on that day, and until then it fails the run for the accident above rather than writing it down.

cases.reason: the only certificate source is an x5u (label 35), which is a reference and not evidence: nothing in the message certifies the signing key
cases.headers: x5u with a URI that resolves for nobody, and no x5chain
cases.description: An x5u naming a URI, and no x5chain: the message says where its certificate may be found instead of carrying it. The URI is under `.invalid`, which resolves for nobody [RFC 2606 §2], so no run of this suite reaches anything. Both refuse. This is the one row in the family with no measured opening — a verifier that fetched would fail here too, so the row cannot separate declining to fetch from trying and not arriving. What it pins is the verdict, which is worth pinning: an implementation that began verifying this message would show up here. The abstention itself is argued from the code and not from this row: COSE.TS calls a URI "a fetch, which a signature library has no business performing", and in Styx nothing reads the label.

The sound chain in x5chain and an x5u beside it, pointing at a URI that resolves for nobody. Nothing here needs fetching: every certificate the message is about is in it. An implementation that treats a header it does not read as fatal refuses this message, and so does one that tries the URI and takes the failure for an error — which makes this row the family's fetch detector, as far as a suite with no network can have one. `normative` on RFC 9052 §3, the same sentence as the bag row: what a verifier need not understand it must ignore.

cases.reason: crit names label 35 and neither implementation understands x5u, and RFC 9052 §3.1 gives a verifier that cannot process a critical header nothing to do but refuse
cases.description: The bag row's question for the other label: `crit: [35]` beside the x5u and the sound chain. Both refuse, and the row above shows the same message verifying without the crit. `normative` since 2026-11-02 on the same sentence of RFC 9052 §3.1, and with the cleaner opening of the two: the row above is this message minus the crit entry, header for header, and it verifies, so what is refused here is the demand and nothing else. An implementation that fetched certificates would understand label 35 and would be right to accept, and would make this a row to read again.

cases.headers: Countersignature0 version 2 (label 12), made with the key of strangerMeter, beside the chain
cases.description: The sound chain in x5chain, and in the unprotected bucket a `Countersignature0 version 2` [RFC 9338, label 12]: a bare ESB256 signature over the Countersign_structure of Section 3.3, the context "CounterSignature0V2", the body's protected bucket, no external data, the payload and the body's signature, made with the key of the corpus's `strangerMeter`, a second party certified by the same authority, and verified by the generator before the file is written. Both implementations carry the name and neither reads it: COSE.TS leaves it out of scope because its algorithm and key "travel outside the message, by agreement", and in Styx it is a constant nothing else reads. An implementation that treats a header it does not read as fatal refuses this message. One that read it, with the algorithm and the key from its context as RFC 9338 says, would verify it as well, because the countersignature is sound. So the row holds whoever implements what. `normative` on the sentence of RFC 9052 §3 the bag and URI rows of §26 stand on. There is no `crit` row beside it: `crit` names protected header parameters and this one is unprotected, so `crit: [12]` would be refused for naming a label absent from the protected bucket, which cose-crit already asks.

cases.headers: counter signature (label 7) of RFC 8152, made with the key of strangerMeter, beside the chain
cases.description: The sound chain in x5chain, and in the unprotected bucket the `counter signature` of RFC 8152 [label 7]: a COSE_Signature whose protected bucket names ESB256, signed over the Sig_structure of RFC 8152 Section 4.4 with the context "CounterSignature", the body's protected bucket, its own, no external data and the payload. Like the row above it is made with the key of the corpus's `strangerMeter` and verified by the generator before the file is written. Unlike it, it does not cover the body's signature, which is the flaw RFC 9338 replaced it for. RFC 9052 §3.1 still says the label "must be understood by new implementations, to remain compatible with senders that adhere to" RFC 8152. Styx reads and verifies it since fb3314be; COSE.TS carries the name and reads nothing. The verdict on the body asks only what the row above asks, whether a header nobody reads may cost a sound message its verification, and both verify. `normative` on the same sentence. Whether a verifier also processes the countersignature is what RFC 9052 asks, and no verdict on the body can show it, so the row asks it separately: `countersignature` names whose key it must verify under, the certificate `strangerMeter` of the corpus, and each implementation is asked whether it does. That second question is `survey`, because the "must" is lowercase and the label deprecated, and an implementation that reads no label 7 answers it by saying so. There is no `crit` row for the same reason as above, and besides, RFC 9052 §3.1 says labels 0 to 7 "SHOULD be omitted" from crit.

The control of this family, and the one whose bytes carry the most: they are byte for byte the message both implementations produce and agree on for `cose-x509:chain-signed-with-rsa`, and the generator refuses to write this file unless it reproduces them. So the RSA written out in this file — from the modular exponentiation and the EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 encoding up, because the noble packages have none — makes the same 256 octets two independent implementations make, and the certificate it mints with the parameter the corpus has comes out as the corpus certificate itself, which the generator also refuses to write this file without. Both pins matter more here than in the families above, because this is the one family that signs: without them the two rows below would be refusals of whatever this generator got wrong about RSA or about DER.

cases.reason: the signature algorithm carries a zero-length OCTET STRING where RFC 4055 §5 requires a NULL or nothing, and the certificate is consistent in it: both copies carry it and the issuer's signature covers one of them
cases.parameters: a zero-length OCTET STRING, beside sha256WithRSAEncryption
cases.description: The row §28 recorded as not measured, now minted. `sha256WithRSAEncryption` with a zero-length OCTET STRING beside it instead of the NULL — in both of the copies a certificate holds, with the issuer's signature made again over the body that holds one of them, so the certificate is sound in every respect but the one it is about. That consistency is why the row needed a third encoder: patching a minted certificate reaches only an inconsistent one, which both implementations refuse, and the refusals say so. Measured here: Bouncy Castle reads this certificate, reports its parameters as `04 00`, and verifies the signature, so Styx verified this message until 82af43fd; since then it refuses it as well, where it reads the chain, next to the DER check. COSE.TS refuses it at the parse, saying the identifier "carries parameters … where RFC 4055 allows a NULL or nothing at all". So the row that was a divergence is an agreement now, and it is `normative` since 2026-11-04 by the maintainer's decision. RFC 4055 §5 says the parameters MUST be NULL, so nothing here is a valid certificate and refusing it is right. Nothing in RFC 4055 or RFC 9360 is addressed to a verifier of COSE messages, so this is a requirement of this suite: a third implementation that verified the message would fail here for being lenient about a field it does not interpret, and not for breaking a rule addressed to it.

The same identifier with no parameters after it — the AlgorithmIdentifier two octets shorter, the TBSCertificate's own length redone, the signature made over the result. This is the encoding RFC 4055 §2 calls "the correct encoding", and §5 puts the requirement on the reader in its own words: "Implementations MUST accept the parameters being absent as well as present." So the row is `normative` on a sentence rather than on a reading, and it is the one that gives the row above its meaning: without it a refusal there could be a reader that simply demands the NULL, where the pair shows exactly where each side draws its line. Both accept. COSE.TS accepts absent parameters by a decision in `expectNoParameters` and not by omission, which is what this row holds it to; Bouncy Castle reports the parameters as null and verifies.

cases.keyType: id-RSASSA-PSS, with parameters naming SHA-256, over a message signed with PS256
cases.description: The control of this family: the key is restricted to RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 and the message is signed with PS256, which is that. It is also the family's one anchor for the signing, because no row in this suite carries a PSS signature these bytes could be compared against — a PSS signature is salted, and Bouncy Castle draws its salt from a random this file cannot reproduce. So what says the signature is right is that both implementations verify this message, measured rather than pinned; the certificate is pinned the other way, by reminting it with the identifier the corpus has and requiring `rsaMeter` back octet for octet. Without this row the four beside it would prove nothing: a message refused by everybody is refused whatever anybody checks.

cases.reason: the certificate restricts the key to RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 and the message is signed with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, which no key named by id-RSASSA-PSS is for
cases.keyType: id-RSASSA-PSS, with parameters naming SHA-256, over a message signed with RS256
cases.description: The row the key type exists for. The same certificate as the control, with the message signed PKCS #1 v1.5 instead — and the key is an RSA key, so the signature is perfectly good arithmetic that an implementation reading `rsaEncryption` would verify without hesitating, which is what makes refusing it an answer. What forbids it is one sentence about intent: id-RSASSA-PSS is in the subject public key info "when the RSA private key owner wishes to limit the use of the public key exclusively to RSASSA-PSS" [RFC 4055 §3.1]. Measured: COSE.TS attaches the PS256 the parameters name to the key and then refuses the message for stating another algorithm; Bouncy Castle hands Styx an RsaKeyParameters that is indistinguishable from the control's, keeping the identifier on the certificate structure and not on the key, so Styx verifies. `survey`: the restriction is real and RFC 4055 states it, and it states it as what the owner wishes rather than as what a verifier must enforce, and RFC 9360 says nothing about it at all. Which of the two a verifier should be is for the specification to settle rather than for this suite.

cases.reason: the certificate restricts the key to RSASSA-PSS with SHA-384 and the message is signed with PS256, and RFC 4055 §3.3 requires the signature's parameters to be the key's
cases.keyType: id-RSASSA-PSS, with parameters naming SHA-384, over a message signed with PS256
cases.description: The same question one level finer, and the one RFC 4055 answers with a MUST rather than with a wish. The scheme agrees — the key is for RSASSA-PSS and the message is RSASSA-PSS — and the hash does not: the key names SHA-384 and PS256 hashes with SHA-256. Scenario 3 of §3.3 says all parameters of the signature must match the key's but the salt length, which this message's do not. The parameter set is Bouncy Castle's own, lifted out of `rsaPssManufacturerCA`, so nothing here turns on this generator's idea of how to write one. Measured: COSE.TS attaches PS384 and refuses PS256 beside it. Styx verified it until 2041ccbc, because Bouncy Castle keeps the identifier on the certificate and not on the key, and since then reads the restriction from the certificate and refuses as well. So the row that was a divergence is an agreement now, and it is `normative` since 2026-11-04 by the maintainer's decision: the half of the pair with a MUST behind it, so an implementation that verifies this message breaks RFC 4055 rather than declining an option.

cases.keyType: id-RSASSA-PSS, with parameters asking for a salt of 20, over a message signed with PS256
cases.description: The other half of scenario 3, and the one field a key and a signature are read differently for. "The saltLength field in the signature parameters MUST be greater or equal to that in the key parameters field" [RFC 4055 §3.3] — so the key states a floor and not a width, and this key asks for twenty octets, which is also what the DEFAULT of §3.1 gives. PS256 signs with a salt as long as its hash [RFC 8230 §2], which is 32, and 32 is above 20, so the message is one this key is for. Both accept. The row is here because an implementation that read a key's parameters the way it reads a signature's would require the 32 and refuse a certificate the specification allows — and nothing else in this suite would notice, every parameter set Bouncy Castle writes asking for exactly the hash's width. These are Bouncy Castle's bytes with one octet lowered, so what the row turns on is the twenty and nothing else.

cases.keyType: id-RSASSA-PSS, with no parameters, over a message signed with PS256
cases.description: The identifier alone, which is scenario 2 of §3.3: "The key is identified by the id-RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm identifier, but the parameters field is absent. In this case no parameter validation is needed." This is also the one place in a certificate where that identifier may stand without parameters at all — beside a signature value they "MUST be present" — so a reader that learned to require them from the signature side refuses this certificate, and both of these accept it. `normative` on that sentence, and the shorter certificate besides: the AlgorithmIdentifier is two octets smaller than `rsaEncryption`'s, where the parameterised ones are 52 larger, so the three rows of this family move the subject public key info's length in both directions.

cases.reason: the certificate restricts the key to RSASSA-PSS, naming no hash, and the message is signed with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5
cases.keyType: id-RSASSA-PSS, with no parameters, over a message signed with RS256
cases.description: The second row's question with the parameters gone, and the one row here where both implementations are lenient together — which is why it is written down rather than required. Measured: both verify this message. Styx for the reason it verifies the second row, and COSE.TS for a different one it states in its own changelog: the restriction here is to a scheme and not to an algorithm, and the COSE algorithms bundle a scheme with a hash, so "RSASSA-PSS with whichever hash" is not a name it has to attach to the key — a key would have to carry a family instead. So this row and the second one together say where the enforcement comes from: from the parameters naming a hash, and not from the identifier. `survey`, and `reject` in it is what honouring §3.1 would mean rather than what this suite asks of anyone. It is also the shape §25 warns about — two implementations lenient at once, which recording catches and requiring nothing does not — and the reason it is recorded and not promoted is that §3.1 puts the restriction in the key owner's wishes and no specification here turns it into a verifier's duty.
